subsystems.name: Micro airframe
subsystems.role: carries the pollen tip to a specific flower and hovers there long enough to make contact.
parts: brushless motors and propellers, or flapping-wing actuators

subsystems.name: Pollen transfer tip
subsystems.role: picks pollen up from one flower and releases it onto the stigma of another without bruising either.
parts: gel or adhesive coating, or an electrostatic charging electrode
quick-release mount so the tip can be cleaned or replaced

subsystems.name: Perception system
subsystems.role: finds open, pollen-receptive flowers and positions the tip within a millimetre or two.
parts: onboard or offboard computer running a flower detector
height and proximity sensor to stop the drone crashing into petals

subsystems.name: Flight control and autonomy
subsystems.role: flies slow, precise paths down crop rows instead of fast point-to-point flight.
parts: position hold (RTK satellite navigation or visual odometry)
obstacle avoidance for stems, trellis wire and people
mission planner that maps which flowers have already been visited

subsystems.name: Swarm coordination
subsystems.role: one drone cannot pollinate a field, so dozens must work a block together.
parts: base station or docking perch with battery swap or recharge

subsystems.name: Pollen supply and handling
subsystems.role: pollen is living material that must stay viable and be matched to the right variety.
parts: loading or refilling of the tip

buildSteps.title: Set a mass and airtime budget
buildSteps.detail: Everything follows from this: a drone light enough to hover precisely over a flower for a few minutes, with battery, camera and tip included.

buildSteps.title: Design the pollen tip
buildSteps.detail: Choose bristle stiffness and length, then test coatings — an adhesive gel or an electrostatic charge — to see which picks up the most pollen and releases it on contact. Pollen grains are tens of micrometres across and easily damaged.

buildSteps.title: Prove it on single flowers
buildSteps.detail: In a greenhouse or lab, hover over one flower, touch the tip to the anthers, then touch it to another flower's stigma, and count pollen grains transferred under a microscope. A 2017 experiment in Japan used a small quadcopter with horsehair bristles wetted with an ionic-liquid gel to move pollen between lily flowers.

buildSteps.title: Build the flower detector
buildSteps.detail: Photograph thousands of flowers at different stages, label which are open and receptive, and train a vision model to find them and aim the tip. Cherry, apple and kiwi flowers all look different, so models are crop-specific.

buildSteps.title: Automate a whole plant
buildSteps.detail: Fly a full tree or plant, visit every suitable flower in sequence, and log which were skipped. Fruit set on the drone-visited branches is then compared with bee-visited and hand-pollinated controls.

buildSteps.title: Run field trials
buildSteps.detail: Move to an orchard or greenhouse row, fly within wind and daylight limits, and measure the share of flowers that set fruit and the quality of the fruit — this is the only number that matters commercially.

buildSteps.title: Scale to a swarm
buildSteps.detail: Multiply to tens or hundreds of units working one block, with docking stations for recharging. Coverage, not flight, is the limiting factor: a field has hundreds of thousands of flowers per hectare.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture cheaply enough
buildSteps.detail: Pollination drones will be lost to wind, rain and collisions, so they must cost a few dollars each — injection-moulded frames, printed circuit boards, robot assembly, and no exotic parts.

prerequisites.why: flapping-wing robots the size of an insect and small quadcopters both fly, but short flight time and drift make millimetre-precise hovering hard outdoors.
today's small drones fly for minutes, so a field-scale operation needs frequent recharging or docking.
vision models can find open flowers in controlled conditions; doing it reliably in a real orchard canopy, in sunlight and wind, is not solved.
pollen loses fertility within hours to days and must be kept cool and dry. Hand pollination of date palms and kiwifruit already runs a pollen industry that drones could plug into.
knowing when each variety is receptive decides whether drone visits happen at the right time of day at all.

pathway.milestone: single-flower demonstrations in greenhouses and lab testbeds
pathway.unlocks: proof that a machine can move viable pollen without destroying the flower.

pathway.milestone: greenhouse pollination services for high-value crops such as tomatoes and strawberries
pathway.unlocks: a first commercial niche, because indoor rows are wind-free, mapped and already use purchased bumblebee hives.

pathway.milestone: supplementing bees in orchards, targeted at varieties or hot spells where bee visits fall short
pathway.unlocks: a role alongside pollinators rather than instead of them.

pathway.milestone: a managed field-scale pollination service priced per hectare
pathway.unlocks: a hedge for growers if wild and managed pollinators keep declining.

pathway.milestone: selective cross-pollination to set specific varieties
pathway.unlocks: a quality tool, not just a rescue measure, since drones can be programmed to carry one variety's pollen to another.
